lesson_title: The Truce in the Tin: Optimisation and Rates of Change
hook_text: Why are tins squat instead of tall? Calculus signed the truce — and the same trick finds the biggest kraal one roll of fence can hold.
clip_script: One roll of fencing, 160 metres, and a long farm wall you can borrow for free. Fence a skinny ribbon and it holds nothing. Blow the whole roll on two deep sides and there is nothing left for the front — nothing again. Somewhere between the silly extremes hides the biggest kraal, and calculus walks straight to it. Call the width x: the front gets 160 minus two x, and the area is x times that — a frowning parabola. The top of the frown is where the slope is zero. Differentiate: 160 minus four x. Zero at x equals 40. Width 40, front 80, three thousand two hundred square metres — no guessing, no tables. Now flip it: a tin must hold 108 cubic centimetres using the least metal. Wide tin: huge base, cheap walls. Tall tin: tiny base, endless walls. The cheapest design is the truce between the two costs, where the material curve runs flat: base 6 by 6, height 3 — half as tall as it is wide. Squat. Exactly like the tins on a shop shelf. That is optimisation: write the formula, spend the constraint, differentiate, and let zero slope find the best design on earth.
visual_style: A fence roll unspooling against a farm wall, the rectangle morphing from ribbon to deep strip while an area meter rises and falls, then a tin stretching tall and squashing flat as a material-cost curve bottoms out at the squat shape.
mood: Practical, sly, satisfying — everyday objects revealing hidden mathematics.
pacing: Two quick failure beats, a calm derivative reveal, then the tin morphing to its winning shape on the final beat.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and learn the four-step recipe that finds the best of anything.
